title: Over-Engineering and Pattern-Happy Design
summary: Recognizing when a design applies patterns and abstraction for their own sake, at a real cost to today's readers, and how to call it out constructively in review.

slides.markdown:
**Over-engineering** is the mirror image of most anti-patterns in this group: instead of too little structure, it's too much — solving a problem you don't have yet, at a real cost to the person reading the code today. A factory that only ever produces one implementation, a plugin system with one plugin, an interface with exactly one caller — all pay abstraction's cost with none of its benefit yet.

This topic is about recognizing pattern-happy design, understanding why it feels like good engineering while you're doing it, and pushing back on it constructively in review.

slides.sectionTitle: Over-engineering defined: cost paid today for a problem you don't have yet
slides.markdown:
**Over-engineering** means adding flexibility, abstraction, or configurability for requirements that are speculative rather than real — "we might need to swap the database later" when there's no concrete plan or driver to do so. The defining trait isn't that the extra structure is *useless forever*; it's that its cost is paid immediately (more files, more indirection, more onboarding time) while its benefit is deferred to a maybe-future that may never arrive.

The honest cost accounting: every layer of abstraction is a tax on every future reader, paid whether or not the flexibility is ever used. If it's never used, the entire tax was pure loss.

slides.sectionTitle: Symptoms: a factory with one product, a strategy with one strategy
slides.markdown:
The tell-tale symptoms are countable, not vibes-based. A **factory** class that has only ever produced one concrete type since it was written. A **strategy interface** with exactly one implementation, injected everywhere "in case we need a second one." An **interface** with exactly one class implementing it and exactly one caller, where the interface adds a layer of indirection without enabling a second implementation to actually exist.

Each of these is a form of unnecessary indirection — a generalization abstracted before there was a second concrete case to generalize *from*. That's the practical test for premature abstraction: can you point to two real, current call sites that need different behavior? If not, the abstraction is speculative.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a simple requirement buried under four layers of indirection
slides.markdown:
![A welcome-email requirement passing through four stacked layers of indirection before reaching the one line that actually calls sendEmail()](assets/indirection-stack.svg)

Each layer in the stack exists to support a variation that doesn't occur anywhere in the codebase — one factory, one handler, one builder, one visitor, each with a single concrete case running through it.

The practical cost: a new engineer implementing "also send a welcome SMS" has to read and understand four files before writing the one line that actually matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Why pattern-happy design feels like good engineering — and why that instinct misleads
slides.markdown:
Applying a named design pattern feels like doing the job well: it demonstrates you know Factory, Strategy, and Visitor, and the resulting code *looks* professionally structured, with named interfaces and clean separation. That feeling is real, and it's exactly why the mistake is so common among engineers who care about quality — this isn't laziness, it's the opposite instinct pointed the wrong way.

The miscalibration is judging code by how sophisticated its structure looks rather than by how well its structure matches the problem's actual current shape. A junior developer solving today's one-case problem with a plain function is, by this measure, sometimes doing better engineering than a senior one wrapping it in four patterns for a second case that may never exist.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: appropriate abstraction vs speculative generality
slides.markdown:
| | Appropriate abstraction | Speculative generality |
|---|---|---|
| Driven by | Two or more real, current call sites needing different behavior | An imagined future need, not yet real |
| Cost paid | Now, in exchange for a benefit also realized now | Now, in exchange for a benefit that may never arrive |
| Typical origin | Extracted after duplication actually appears | Designed in upfront, before any duplication exists |
| Review response | Usually accepted without much debate | Worth a direct question: "what's the second case?" |

**How to decide:** ask whether a second concrete case exists *today*. If yes, the abstraction is paying for something real; if it's purely anticipated, the interface can be added later, when the second case actually shows up — that's cheaper than guessing wrong now.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: justifying complexity with "we might need this later"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Let's add this abstraction now — we might need to support a second payment provider later, so building it flexible from the start saves rework."

**Why it's wrong:** "we might need this later" is unfalsifiable — it can justify nearly any amount of speculative structure, because almost anything *might* be needed eventually. Without a concrete, near-term driver (a signed contract with the second provider, a roadmap item with a date), the abstraction is a bet made with no real information about what the actual second case will look like — and premature abstractions are often shaped wrong for the real requirement when it finally arrives, meaning the flexibility gets thrown away anyway.

**Correct model:** this is the core of YAGNI — build for the requirement you actually have, and add the abstraction when the second real case shows up, informed by what that case actually needs rather than a guess made months earlier.

slides.sectionTitle: Calling it out in code review without being adversarial
slides.markdown:
The goal in review is to surface unnecessary complexity as a genuine question, not a verdict — "this is over-engineered" reads as a judgment of the author, while "what's the second implementation this interface is designed for?" reads as a real question with a real answer, good or bad. If the author has one in mind, you've learned something and the abstraction is probably fine. If they don't, they've usually just talked themselves out of it.

Other useful framings: "what would break if we deleted this factory and called the constructor directly?" and "can we ship the simple version now and extract this if a second case actually shows up?" Each invites the author to justify the complexity on its merits, rather than putting them in a position of defending a design choice against a flat dismissal.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level nuance: prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction
slides.markdown:
There's a sharper version of "wait for the second case" that experienced engineers reach for once duplication actually shows up: sometimes two similar-looking pieces of code are duplicated *because they represent genuinely different concepts that happen to look alike today*, not because someone forgot to extract a shared function — and abstracting them together couples two things that should be allowed to evolve independently. This is Sandi Metz's well-known framing: **duplication is far cheaper to undo than the wrong abstraction**. Deleting a copy-pasted function is a local, mechanical change; unwinding a shared abstraction that two callers have grown to depend on differently — after one of them needed a behavior the other didn't — usually means a wider, riskier refactor touching every call site.

The practical test before merging two similar code paths: ask whether they're the same thing that will always change together, or two things that merely look similar *right now* because neither has needed to diverge yet. Validation logic for a `User` signup form and a `User` profile-edit form might look identical today and still be the wrong thing to share, if a future requirement (email verification required only at signup) will need to split them apart anyway.

This directly informs the review question from the previous slide: "what's the second implementation" isn't just about whether a second case *exists* — it's about whether the two cases are actually the same concept, or coincidentally similar code that's about to be forced apart the first time either one changes.
